_: One run of any command. The same shape for fix, ship, sprint and epic — what differs is which fields are filled. Written by the run, read by the run that resumes it, by the reviewer, and by whatever launched it. JSON because a script reads it; the owner reads the pull request instead.
_records: Every field drawn below as `[{ … }]` is a list of records and is read as one — `tasks`, `assumptions`, `answers`, `review.findings`. Filling one with sentences leaves a field that looks answered to a person and is empty to everything that reads it; the check names a run file that does.
_step: queued | design | build | verify | deliver | done | blocked | skipped — and building | closing, which only a driver writes on a batch's own file while it works through the children, and gate | auditing | proving, which only `epic` writes on its own file as it moves between its phases. The last three of the first list are terminal: a driver stops watching a run that reaches one, so nothing may leave it there while still working. The list is closed, and the check names a step outside it.
_parent: The run this one continues from, when a batch chains its features. Its run file carries the decisions this one inherits; its branch is this one's base. Inside a batch the driver sets it to the last child that was actually built, so a feature never inherits a branch that does not exist.
_needs: Which of the batch's other features this one cannot be built without, by slug. It decides one thing: whether this feature is skipped when another fails. `[]` says somebody looked and there are none; **left out it means nobody looked**, and the driver falls back to the feature before it in the queue, which is what a chained batch has always assumed. Written by the composing session when the owner named the order, or by the driver from the frame child's map; read by the driver and by nothing else. Never the same as `base`: every child still branches off the last one built, because that is what makes integration a property of the chain rather than a step at the end.
_deliver: pr — open one at the end, the default. branch — push and stop, because a batch delivers its features together.
_session: The session this run is being built in, written by the driver when it starts one. The stop hook matches on it and on nothing else — a run with no session is a run no hook has an opinion about.
approach: one sentence: how this is being built here
seams: the points the tests sit at
_tasks: The run's own plan, written at Design and closed one at a time. Each task is the smallest unit that carries its own verification, because the commit is the boundary a session is cut at: a driver that asks a long run to hand over says `finish the task you are on`, and half a task is the one thing the next session cannot pick up. `commit` is what makes that checkable rather than promised — the SHA that closed the task, written in the same movement as `done: true`. It is asked for by the check, resolved against this run's own branch, and read by the reviewer, which otherwise has to find a task's work by walking the whole diff. A task whose change rode along in a neighbour's commit names that neighbour's SHA; that is a fact, not a breach. Written by the run, read by the session that resumes it and by `agent-kit:reviewer`, closed by nobody — it dies with the run directory.
_unmet: Tests this run left marked `agent-kit:unmet` — a promise of the entry the product does not keep. One line each: the entry, what the code does instead, and what it waits for. The closing session reads only run files, so a mark left out of here does not reach the batch's pull request.
_deferred: Work this run decided not to do, one line each — the same lines it wrote into docs/technical_debt.md. Filled inside a batch, where the closing session carries them into the ledger; delivering its own pull request, a run has already written them there and leaves this empty.
_closed_debt: Items of docs/technical_debt.md this run finished and deleted from the file, one line each. The ledger only shrinks in a commit that does the work, and this is where a batch's report gets the count from.
_finish: An epic's own plan, settled at its gate and never asked again — bar `lenses`, which the audit phase writes — a resumed run reads it instead of putting the same questions a second time. `scope`: the entry keys taken, which is `entries` above; this says which list they came from. `lenses`: the audit lenses this product needs — written not at the gate but by the `--advance` that reaches the audit, which has seen the product built; empty means not chosen yet. `waves`: how many times a lens may be re-run after its findings are fixed, before the remainder goes to the report — a lens is never run twice over unchanged code, so a wave is always audit, then the sprints that fix it, then the audit again. `built`: the batches already delivered, so an advance knows where it is.
_model: Which model this run's session is started on — an alias like `opus` or `sonnet`, or a full name. Left out, the session takes whatever the install defaults to; a brief or an epic's gate writes the model it is itself running on, so children inherit the owner's choice without being asked. The driver sets it by typing `/model` into the session before the task, so it works however the session was launched.
_window: The tmux session the owner briefed this run in, so a driver knows where to put its news. Only a batch has one, and a batch without one simply runs unnarrated.
_waiting_on: The fork this run is stopped on, in its own words — cleared when the answer lands in `answers`. A driver, the window and `next` all read this to know a run is waiting and on what; it is the only route by which a night's question reaches a phone.
_answers: What the owner was asked and what they answered, verbatim — one entry per question. A run that resumes reads this instead of asking again, and the pull request quotes it instead of remembering it.
_review: What the reviewer found and what became of it. `verdict` is its closing sentence. `findings` is a list of records, never of sentences: `severity` and `closed` are what holds a run to finishing with no critical or major one open, and a line of prose carrying the same words in it says nothing to the program that checks. `security` says whether that pass ran, and when it did not, why not.
_suite: What was run and what it returned: tests, types, lint — and, when the feature has a surface a person can reach, what was opened in the running application and what was seen there. 'Not exercised' is an answer; silence is not.
_proved_at: The commit the suite above was last run on — `git rev-parse HEAD`, written whenever `suite` is written and rewritten every time it is run again. Everything else in this file is the run's own word for what happened; this is the one field that binds a claim to a tree, and without it a suite that passed three commits ago reads exactly like one that passed on what is being delivered. The check names a finished run that recorded a result and no tree, and one whose tree is not in this repository at all. Asked of the runs that ran a suite and of no others — never of a child carrying its own `prompt`, which has no suite, and never of a batch's own file, whose `suite` is what its children reported from trees it never stood on.
_mutation: What `commands.mutate` returned over this feature's own files — `{files}` in it is replaced by the run with what it changed against its base: `killed` and `survived` as numbers, `command` as it was actually run, which is also what makes `why` an answer rather than a sentence. This is the only evidence in the kit that a test can fail — everything else about a test is the word of the session that wrote it, and a test written after the code and never seen red asserts whatever the code already did. `why` instead of the numbers when it did not run: no `commands.mutate` in `project.yml`, or the tool would not start. Never left null on a finished run, because a run that skipped it and a run that passed it must not read alike. Survivors are a finding for the pull request, not a blocker: some mutations change nothing a person could observe, and a night that stops over one has cost more than the tests are worth.
_frame: The one thing a frame child leaves for a program: which of the batch's features cannot be built without which, `{ "<child slug>": ["<child slug it needs>"] }`. Everything else that child produces is prose, and prose goes under `stack.md` as a `[frame …]` block, where every `ship` already reads it — a second run file nobody opens would reach nobody. The driver applies this map once, the moment that child is built: it writes each `needs`, then re-sorts the batch's `children`. A feature it does not name gets `[]`, because the child was asked about all of them and saying nothing about one is an answer. It may not name a feature outside this batch. Written by the frame child, read by the driver, closed by nothing — it dies with the run directory.
_prompt: What the driver types into this child's session. Left out, it is `/agent-kit:ship --run <this directory>`, which is what a feature is. A batch may hold a child that is not a ship — an audit between two rounds of fixes, a review — and this is how it says so. Everything else is unchanged: the child keeps this run file, and a terminal `step` is still the only signal the driver watches, so a command with no run file of its own must be told here to close one. **A command and this directory, and nothing else.** Two rules, and both were paid for on one live run where thirteen of sixteen children were started by two to five kilobytes of prose somebody composed on the spot. **Name a command, never a file:** a slash command resolves whatever kit is installed, while a path resolves to the plugin cache of the session that wrote it — that run pinned three different versions in one night, so its children read rules three weeks apart. **And what the child must know goes in fields, not in the prompt:** its area is `entries`, everything the command itself does not already say is `task`, and both are read by whoever resumes it. Prose here is read once, by one session, and is gone. The check names a prompt that is briefing rather than invoking.
_spent: What this run cost, written by the driver and by nothing else: `hours` of wall-clock, `features` built, `sessions` started. In these units and not in tokens or money, because those are what an owner can hold against a plan — and because a gate that prices a scope out of prose was measured four times under with nothing to correct it. A batch resumed adds to what it already spent rather than replacing it.
_handoff: What one session of this run leaves for the next one, when the driver asks it to hand over — everything else it knew is in the fields above, in the commits, or was never worth carrying. Four answers and nothing else, under 2000 characters: where you stopped (which task, what is committed, what is still in the tree) **and the files you were working in, by path** — measured, a session that takes a handoff spends 21 turns before its first edit against a fresh one's 33, and what is left of that gap is looking for where the last one was; a path is read in one turn and found in five; what you tried that did not work, and why; what you decided silently that no field holds; what you were about to do next. **Every claim names what proves it — a commit, a green suite, a pushed branch — or says it is unverified.** The next session reads this as a contract and will not re-check it, so a note saying the review is done and must not be run again is either a fact with a commit behind it or a night of work built on a guess; the failure that costs most in long agent work is not a forgotten fact, it is a claim nobody can tell was checked. And never point at a temporary directory: a path under /tmp or a session scratchpad is gone by the time anyone reads it. The session that picks it up moves anything durable into the field that owns it and then empties this — a note left standing is a note the next handoff is mistaken for, and it is what the stop hook reads to know this run stopped on purpose.
_manual: What only the owner can do: a secret and where it goes, an account somewhere, a device to hold, a production environment to fill in. Written by the run that found it, read by the closing session and by `accept`, closed by the owner doing it. Nothing a script can do belongs here — a migration, a build argument, a port, a file mode go into `commands.run` — and neither does a setting that already works, which is an assumption. `proof` is how the owner tells it worked; without it the line is a chore rather than a step. `when`: before_run | before_merge | before_release. Measured on one run, nineteen of these were listed and six genuinely needed a person; the six were unfindable because the list lived in prose and was re-derived at every hand-over.
_notes: Anything this run wants to leave behind that no field above holds — context for whoever picks it up, a dead end worth not repeating, a suspicion. Free prose, read by people and by the closing session. It exists so that no run invents a key of its own: an invented key is one nothing will ever read, because every reader knows only this shape.
